stories.headline: Harry Kane arrival would be 'fulfilment of a dream' - MLS commissioner
stories.summary: MLS commissioner Don Garber would love Harry Kane to follow Lionel Messi across the pond and says the England skipper's interest helps fulfil a dream that Sir David Beckham kept alive.
stories.body:
MLS commissioner Don Garber would love Harry Kane to follow Lionel Messi across the pond and says the England skipper's interest helps fulfil a dream that Sir David Beckham kept alive.

The 33-year-old is in the running for the Ballon d'Or having scored 73 goals for club and country in a season that saw the striker win the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich before World Cup bronze.

Kane shows no signs of slowing and he marked his record-equalling 125th England appearance by extending his international goal tally to 91 in Tuesday's 3-0 Nations League win against Czechia.

The striker scored six goals across a four-match camp that began with him revealing his interest in eventually moving to MLS as the striker spoke about his dreams of being an NFL kicker.

"I'd love for him to do that," commissioner Garber said. "I think, for me, it is the fulfilment of the dream that we had to build a proper soccer league that would drive a soccer nation. That sounds colloquial but actually we have that written down.

"We wanted to create something that would have the Harry Kanes of the world say 'I'd kind of like to play in MLS.' And I think Messi proved that.

"That was a competitive process, working to ensure that we had a dynamic that would be better than going back to Barca, working a dynamic that would not have him want to play in Saudi Arabia.

"Play in Miami, have them be able to build a new stadium and have him set records and be an MVP, and then have an unbelievable goodbye [this week] from his international career."

Garber welcomes Kane's keenness to move to MLS and is eternally grateful to another England captain as he prepares to step down from the post of commissioner he has held since 1999.

Beckham's move to LA Galaxy acted as the catalyst for the league's growth, which only accelerated when the former midfielder helped form Inter Miami and sign Argentina great Messi in 2023.

"I don't think I would say one is more important than the other," Garber said of the star duo's impact.

"David put this league on the path to credibility and respect. In the prime of his career, he came to LA.

"He came into Major League Soccer and showed the world that this league can be competitive, it could be respected, it could be fun, it could have great players.

"It attracted [Thierry] Henry and many, many other players right after that, so without David there's probably no Major League Soccer.

"That being said, Major League Soccer would not be the global phenomenon and not be sort of on the hearts and minds of just about anybody in the world without Leo Messi."

Garber will become chairman at the turn of the year and is proud of his legacy with MLS, which was founded as part of the bid to hold the 1994 World Cup in a country that has just co-hosted the largest edition of the tournament.

- Harry Kane is England's greatest ever player - Jude Bellingham

- Harry Kane's England milestones: From his first cap to becoming all-time record goalscorer

- England Nations League takeaways: Kane makes history, Tuchel steadies ship

The 68-year-old says they have made the planet's "biggest commercial market for the sport" during that time and is excited to see how they build on firm foundations.

"We just went from a country road, now we're getting onto the highway," Garber told the Press Association. "And we've got to get better.

"We have to have a league that is more competitive, that has an ability to get into the Club World Cup and win games. Miami won one.

"Not just be there but have people think that an MLS team can compete against other clubs in the world."

stories.headline: WNBA playoffs 2026: After another early exit, what's next for Fever?
stories.summary: Despite a dominant offense and Caitlin Clark's return, the Fever suffered another early playoff exit. What's next for Indiana?
stories.body:
INDIANAPOLIS -- A week ago, ahead of a deciding Game 3 against the Las Vegas Aces, Indiana Fever forward Myisha Hines-Allen laid out the franchise's expectations plainly.

"There's always going to be room for growth, but with how [GM] Amber [Cox] put this team together, it's championship or bust," Hines-Allen said before the game. "We're all trying to win this championship this year."

After a semifinal appearance in 2025, a season in which star Caitlin Clark sat out most of the year injured, hopes were high for 2026.

And sure enough, the Fever had the No. 1 offense in WNBA history, averaging 96.0 points per game in the regular season. Kelsey Mitchell (24.7 points per game) and Clark (22.3) finished ranked No. 2 and No. 3 in points per game and were the highest-scoring teammates in league history.

But throughout, off-court drama surrounded the team. Then a swoon in the final days of the regular season dropped the Fever to the No. 6 seed, facing the defending champion Aces in a best-of-three first round.

After the Game 3 loss, a back-and-forth affair, the Fever were left reckoning with a season that ended earlier than any of them hoped.

Within 48 hours of the season-ending loss, another controversy had developed: After Cox issued a strong defense of the Fever fanbase in her end-of-season availability, Mitchell seemed to contradict it, referencing troubling fan behavior and the intense microscope that comes with playing alongside Clark. It was a fitting conclusion to a season of big dreams and bitter disappointments where the focus could never just be on basketball.

"Not every season's perfect," Aliyah Boston said Saturday after the season's end. "You're going to have your ups and downs, but we really stuck together through it all. Like no matter what. Obviously, when you look back at games that you wish that you didn't drop early, and maybe that would have been a difference. ... But here we are, right? There's nothing we can do right now."

ON THE COURT, at least one half of the Fever's plan went perfectly.
The offense was formidable, and Clark's return went better than anyone could have hoped. Mitchell set the league record for the most points scored (1,086) and the most 3-point field goals (135) while scoring 20-plus points in a WNBA-record 27 consecutive games. Boston was an All-Star for the fourth consecutive year with a career-high 16.1 points per game, grabbed 8.0 rebounds and extended her range beyond the 3-point line and shot 40.6%.

Clark was the first player in the history of the league to score 40-plus points with 10-plus assists in a single game; her five games of 30-plus points and 10-plus assists this season are more than any other player in league history combined. She became the league's first player to record 800-plus points and 300-plus assists in a single season.

Clark called 2026 one of the most fulfilling years of her career. She played more basketball than ever as she rehabbed. She played in Team USA camps, 40 regular-season games and was selected for the FIBA World Cup team that won gold in September. A worrisome back issue flared up early in the season but proved not to be a long-term issue. The defensive part of her game was highly criticized early in the season as teams specifically targeted her, but even that improved incrementally. A sneaky midrange game began to appear as the season went on to complement the drives to the basket and the step-back 3s.

Clark's first signature shoe with Nike, the Caitlin 1, released last week.

"I didn't play much last year, but I was able to come out here and put together the best season I've had," Clark said, "and perform at a really high level and basically get better in every area and still feel like I have so many areas to improve.

"I guess that's the most exciting part moving forward."

The old saying, though, goes that defense wins championships, and that was the problem all season for the Fever. They ranked No. 11 in points allowed per game (90.4) and No. 8 in defensive rating (108.3). The Aces scored 102 and 94 in Game 1 and 3 victories to eliminate Indiana.

And off the court, the Fever were constantly barraged with distractions or drama. For much of the season, it felt like those 40 minutes between the lines -- win or lose -- were the most peaceful, normal times of the summer for this group.

"Obviously, we weathered a lot," Clark said. "There's always so much outside noise and a microscope of how we perform every single day, and a lot of really good moments, a lot of tough moments, too."

SINCE CLARK WAS drafted No. 1 in 2024, the Fever have had an inordinate amount of attention on the organization from both WNBA fans and entities that rarely paid attention to the league in the past. Clark's name was recently, and randomly, brought up in the middle of a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.

It's been a boon for the Fever, who have become the most popular team in the league thanks in large part to her fame -- quickly acknowledged by all those around the team, including Cox.

"The other piece about Caitlin that I never want to take for granted is just what she has meant to our team, what she has meant to the league, and what she's meant to women's basketball," she said. "She remains the tipping point. You look at the ratings and you look at the full buildings, that started in 2024 when she came into the league, and that is because of Caitlin Clark."

But it can also lead to increased scrutiny on Clark and the rest of the team, as happened multiple times this season.

In June, the relationship between Stephanie White and Clark was questioned after the coach was seen in an animated discussion with the point guard during a 16-point loss to the Portland Fire. Both downplayed it as two competitive people in the heat of the moment. Clark and assistant coach Briann January also had fiery interactions on the sideline that begat questions regarding the franchise player and the coaching staff.

The focus on the Fever's play -- and White -- continued throughout the season. Then, in June, Sophie Cunningham kicked off another round of headlines for the Fever. Cunningham, a popular personality on social media and her podcast, has no problem being an agitator. T-shirts featuring her pointing at DeWanna Bonner after a heated game against the Phoenix Mercury in June became a hot commodity at Fever games at home and on the road.

But one moment affected not only the Fever, but the entire league. In an ESPN article published in July, Cunningham discussed, among other things, how to "protect women's sports" and said: "I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that.' I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

It became a seasonlong topic with coaches and players being asked their opinions around the league. Protests both for and against began forming outside arenas when the Fever would play on the road. Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton was suspended from attending five home games after her exchange with a pair of fans who brought signs into Climate Pledge Arena supporting Cunningham with the Fever in town for a road game in late July.

All these issues and more -- 11 Republican lawmakers sent WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert a letter in July demanding the league take "accountability" for "multiple attacks" against Clark -- came to a head just after the All-Star break.

In a game on Aug. 8, Cunningham took a hit around the head and neck on a fast-break layup from DiJonai Carrington. The particularly hard contact started a dustup on the court; Carrington was issued a flagrant 2 and ejected from the game. Moments later, Carrington posted on her Threads account: "WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever." Postgame, White acknowledged it was a hard foul, but said she didn't think Carrington intentionally went for the neck.

Fever fans accused White of not supporting her players. Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith tweeted, "Ok... The @IndianaFever need to let Stephanie White go. No solid coach would ever take the side of the opposing team's player who committed a flagrant foul on one of your own players. Terrible coaching! The Fever need to defend their players."

During the next home game, on Aug. 11 against the New York Liberty, boos rained down on Gainbridge Arena. The disdain was focused on White during pregame introductions. Before that game, White had used her pregame media session to respond to the noise; team president Kelly Krauskopf issued a statement with full support for White that same day.

"The hate, the fearmongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win," White said before the game, pounding her fist on a table multiple times.

"We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," she added. "Every day, these women put their ass on the line. Every day, when they go low, we go high. Love will win, grace will win, humility will win, and kindness will win. I stand by them. I will always stand by them.

"Everybody else can go to hell."

EVERY SEASON WITH Clark on the team will have championship expectations, a side effect of having a generational player on the roster. But every season with Clark, through no fault of her own, also brings a level of outside noise that organizations will have to navigate.

That was evident on Saturday, during Mitchell's end-of-season availability.

Compared with her interviews after the Game 3 loss, the weight seemed lifted from Mitchell's shoulders as she smiled and acknowledged that she would be "selfish" in her approach to unrestricted free agency.

Mitchell -- the Fever's No. 2 player in points and assists, No. 1 in 3-point field goals and No. 4 in steals in franchise history -- said it's hard to play in Indiana due to fan behavior and the intense microscope that comes with playing alongside Clark.

"Showing up every day to compete for fans that may or may not like you is hard," Mitchell said.

Earlier Saturday, in her own availability, Cox had effusively praised Clark and ended her session with a staunch defense of Fever fans that have received criticism for their behavior toward opposing players.

"The attacks on our fanbase have no basis in reality, and they need to stop," she said.

(Former Fever player Brianna Turner, now a member of the Aces, disputed Cox's sentiments on social media. "This is an unequivocally false statement," wrote Turner, who serves as treasurer of the Women's National Basketball Players Association. "Players inside and outside the organization have repeatedly issued complaints with the Fever fanbase. While it's not all Indy fans, it's certainly a trend. To say the attacks have 'no basis in reality' is disingenuous.")

Along with Mitchell, Cunningham, Tyasha Harris and Hines-Allen are all unrestricted free agents this winter -- meaning, like everything in the orbit of the Fever, the offseason could be dramatic.

Cox has said her priority is bringing back Mitchell and keeping the Fever's Big Three together.

Clark's play has made her eligible for the "EPIC" (Exceptional Performance on Initial Contract) provision of the new collective bargaining agreement that allows players to renegotiate the fourth year of their rookie deal and sign a three-year extension. Players that have been named all-WNBA first team or second team are eligible for a max deal or the supermax if named MVP.

"Caitlin has earned the opportunity to sign her EPIC extension, so we're really excited to talk to her and her team about that," Cox said. "She had an MVP-caliber season, and it was wonderful to see coming off of her injury."

As for Cunningham, Cox said the off-court conversations surrounding her will not impact the evaluation of the player. Through the first two months of the season, Cunningham was considered a Sixth Player of the Year candidate before she cooled over the last two months. Both Cox and White pointed to help on the wing as an offseason priority.

"Sophie's had two really productive years for us in terms of shooting the basketball," Cox said. "She is a really solid leader in the locker room, a great connector. She brings levity, but also brings a lot of experience. She's serious and is an important voice in our locker room when we need it. When we really need to lock in.

"She's an unrestricted free agent, so we look forward to having those conversations. Again, she had a really productive year, and we'll see just where things take us."

White, too, will be part of the conversations about the Fever's future. She just finished her second year at the helm, and 2025 was considered an overachievement, advancing to within one game of the Finals with an infirmary ward of a roster. The last five months have been considered a disappointment with a first-round exit and questions swirling around her job stability.

"There were some highlights, and there are things we never need to get better at," Cox said after the season. "We're all going to get in the room and get back to the drawing board and we're going to address some of those and make sure that we're ready to go when next season starts. And that includes Steph and the coaching staff."

"I feel support from the organization, no doubt about that," White said after the season. "At the end of the day, it's their decision about whether I return or not. I'd love the opportunity. I love this this franchise. I have always felt supported from this franchise, and I hope to continue to be the coach."

This all awaits Cox in what will undoubtedly be another busy offseason. A new practice facility is scheduled to open before 2027 training camp. Cox wants to add frontcourt depth to help Boston and Makayla Timpson, and a three-and-D wing is also on the wish list. Despite expectations, the Fever were light on playoff experience and there's optimism that it was gained the hard way. The hope is to continue to develop the young talent, build through the draft and supplement through free agency.

After a season with unfulfilled goals and more drama than anyone was thrilled about, there's an understandable wonder of how much could change.

"When you talk about the noise around this team, I think that's just a product of becoming mainstream," Cox said. "People care. I've been a part of this league for many, many years, and you could have a trade, you could have a bad loss and nobody cared. Nobody was writing about it. Nobody was tweeting about it, and that was bad. Apathy was bad.

"So, what comes with the quote-unquote noise? I would call it just a lot of people caring."

stories.headline: Pep Guardiola set to attend first Man City home game since guilty verdict - sources
stories.summary: Pep Guardiola is expected to attend Manchester City's Champions League fixture against Paris Saint-Germain, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
Pep Guardiola is expected to attend Manchester City's Champions League fixture against Paris Saint-Germain, sources have told ESPN, the club's first home game since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.

Guardiola is set to be in the stands at the Etihad Stadium on Wednesday for the first time since quitting as manager at the end of last season.

The timing of the 55-year-old's return is significant, coming in the wake of the damning verdict in City's case with the Premier League.

In the aftermath of the publication of the independent commission's findings, Guardiola released a statement in support of his former club.

He posted on social media: "I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here more than ever.

"I am, always have been, always will be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters.

"Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."

City have maintained their innocence throughout the process and have filed a formal appeal. Both chairman Khaldoon Al-Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano have insisted publicly that the club will be cleared.

The financial breaches which form the basis of the Premier League's case occured between 2009 and 2018. Guardiola became City boss in 2016 and won 20 trophies during a 10-year spell.

City face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday before returning to the Etihad to play reigning European champions PSG three days later.

stories.headline: The Warriors need Yaxel Lendeborg's fast-tracked development
stories.summary: The Golden State Warriors have high hopes for the No. 11 pick after several failed lottery picks.
stories.body:
THE WEEK PRIOR to training camp, every Golden State Warriors player gathered at Jimmy Butler's mansion in San Diego and competed in a handful of pickup games.

In his lone game paired with Stephen Curry and Draymond Green, rookie wing Yaxel Lendeborg found himself near the elbow during a frontcourt inbound. As the ball was delivered to Green up top, Curry cut toward Lendeborg to set a back screen. Both defenders remained with Curry and Lendeborg, sensing it, slipped backdoor and received a pass from Green for an uncontested dunk.

"'That's all year! All year!'" Green and Curry roared at Lendeborg with ferocity, according to the rookie. "Super loud and aggressive."

In Lendeborg's mind, he made the simple read within the flow, using Curry's gravity for two easy points. It represented something far bigger for Green and Curry. Their newest weapon was already recognizing and leveraging the patterns that make the Warriors' offense hum, signaling a readiness to help the team win before the two franchise legends age out of the league.

"It looked like we had been playing together for a long time," Green said.

On their final draft board in June, the Warriors -- who owned the No. 11 pick -- had Lendeborg and Arizona guard Brayden Burries ranked neck-and-neck, behind the consensus group of prospects up top. If Burries was there, team sources have indicated they would've drafted the 20-year-old combo guard for his upside. He had fans all over the organization.

But the Milwaukee Bucks, selecting 10th, took away that option. The Warriors quickly pivoted to Lendeborg, adding the older prospect they believed fit their immediate timeline and urgency of Curry's final seasons.

"He's massive," Butler said. "Just a big human being."

At 24 years old and 241 pounds, standing 6-foot-9 with a 7-foot-4 wingspan, Lendeborg has the size and power of a mid-prime wing on a Warriors roster that is currently thin and injured at that spot, waiting for Butler and Moses Moody to return from lengthy rehabs for serious knee injuries.

Lendeborg won over Steve Kerr in the predraft process, impressing the Warriors coach during a film session because of his knowledge of the game paired with charisma and his willingness to learn.

"Unbelievably coachable," Kerr said after Tuesday night's preseason win over the Los Angeles Lakers.

The organization has been impressed that, after a long national title run at Michigan that included an MCL and ankle sprain in the NCAA tournament, Lendeborg took his offseason work seriously, played in eight summer league games and led them to a Las Vegas title.

Then he showed up at training camp and Kerr inserted him into the starting lineup, showing a belief that he can be a small forward in a lineup that includes Green and a center or a power forward next to Green in smaller groupings.

Newcomers either typically get the Warriors' unique style, offensive flow and Curry-centric approach or don't -- and it's obvious immediately. Andre Iguodala and Juan Toscano-Anderson did. Kelly Oubre and James Wiseman didn't.

The Warriors' belief in Lendeborg comes at a time when the franchise is desperate for young talent that helps win in Curry's final years while better positioning them for a tricky rebuild.

"He's going to play a ton," Kerr told ESPN. "Frankly, he deserves it. He's one of our best players already."

LENDEBORG INITIALLY DECLARED for the 2025 draft after two seasons at UAB, averaging 17.7 points and 11.4 rebounds as a small-ball center his last season there. General manager Mike Dunleavy and a group of front office members met Lendeborg at the combine in Chicago. Their feedback: He was behaving "like a jackass," Lendeborg recalled in a summer league interview with ESPN.

"I was like, damn, I did that bad?" Lendeborg laughed.

It wasn't clear then whether Lendeborg was even a first-round pick. There was a belief he needed to improve his work habits and sharpen his approach. He withdrew from the draft, transferred to Michigan, morphed into a dominant force on a national title team -- averaging 15.1 points and 6.8 rebounds per game while shooting 51.5% from the field -- and returned to the combine with a rising stock.

"The biggest thing for sure is just practice overall," Lendeborg said. "I never took practice serious [until Michigan]."

Kerr commented recently about Lendeborg's constant presence in the gym. Teammates have embraced what they say is a genuine personality and curiosity, as Lendeborg regularly asks questions to help fast track his growth.

"I don't think he's afraid," Curry said. "It's a lot for a rookie to absorb all this information and process it. He's open-minded. He's listening. You can tell he's locked in mentally."

But there's still a natural "goofiness," as several in the building have described it, that seeps onto the court and will cause inevitable growing pains for the rookie. One possession into the preseason, the referee had to ask Lendeborg to tuck in his jersey. The coaches particularly mention the "nonchalant" nature impacting his defensive focus.

"The biggest thing I see that he needs work with is being in a stance," Kerr said. "Off-ball, he tends to stand up a little bit. The other night against the Clippers, he was casual and Rui (Hachimura) came off a couple pindowns and he wasn't quite prepared."

The Hachimura scouting report is clear -- run him off the line. The Warriors went over it prior to the preseason game against the Clippers. But Lendeborg sagged off and gave him a few jumpers. Green expressed a bit of on-court frustration and reiterated a need for Lendeborg to focus more on the defensive end when the rookie texted the veteran for advice after the first game.

It was also a problem two days prior during an open intrasquad scrimmage. Lendeborg gifted De'Anthony Melton and Gui Santos space on the perimeter and they stepped into easy 3s. Green was frustrated. Someone in the gym had to loudly remind him: "He's a rookie!"

"Everybody (in the NBA) can shoot," Lendeborg said. "I've been a guy that's always given up the jump shot and kind of baited players to go into the paint and attack me. Here I can't do that."

Lendeborg said he became comfortable at Michigan in a switch everything scheme. He's rangy and fluid with shot-blocking instincts and felt comfortable against guards, wings and bigs. But this isn't college.

"The switch attack offense in the NBA is very, very advanced," assistant coach Frank Vogel told ESPN. "So if you're just going to rely only on switching, it's not all about guarding the guy you switched onto. It's about guarding the exchange, giving up roll behinds, giving up hip taps, slip outs."

Vogel was hired this summer to take control of a Warriors defense that has slipped. Players, coaches and front office members have raved about Vogel's early impact and attention to detail. That includes regular lessons for Lendeborg.

"It's more like a chase over, fight over kind of game [in the NBA]," Lendeborg said. "I've never really done that, so I'm still trying to navigate that. Then some of the rotations off-ball as well. Just, like, when to help, when not to help. Those kind of things have been confusing me a little bit."

There are defensive areas where Lendeborg's size will naturally help. He has 18 rebounds in 40 preseason minutes and said after his second game he felt it was easier to rebound in the NBA because the paint isn't as packed and the opposing rebounders seem "lazy."

"In a league where the big shoulder offense of just plowing into a guy to create space, he's going to be one of them guys that you're not going to be able to punk," Vogel said. "And that's going to be a big benefit to us."

Most rookies, as Vogel put it, arrive "really thin" and need at least a couple years in the weight room before it's feasible for them to survive when the NBA game ramps up physically. But Lendeborg is already in the OG Anunoby and Paolo Banchero weight class (240-plus pounds). His body is ready. The veterans and coaches are now just trying to train the mind.

"What does Shai [Gilgeous-Alexander] do?" Kerr said. "What does Damian Lillard do if you get switched on him? You're guarding a big, know the scouting report -- is Chet Holmgren going to pop and hit 3s? What's his tendency? Pick a guy. You get switched on to Luka [Doncic]. Are you ready for that pump fake or is he going to goad you into three free throws? That only comes with experience and watching League Pass and getting to know the league."

THE WARRIORS DON'T have the greatest recent track record of developing lottery rookies, but they believe the timing and situation is far different than it was with Jonathan Kuminga, who the Warriors drafted with the No. 7 pick in 2021 and traded in February after never finding the correct developmental direction and alignment during five turbulent seasons..

Lendeborg is actually a month older than Kuminga. The Warriors drafted Kuminga the same year Lendeborg was beginning the second of three seasons at Arizona Western College in Yuma. His late teens, early 20s growing pains were ironed out in junior college and eventually high-stakes Division I.

Front offices often shy away from drafting older prospects early because of the concern about a limited upside. Lendeborg is already 24. But if he is an immediate high-level contributor at a position of great need, as the Warriors believe he will be, they will get his age 24 to 27 seasons on a bargain four-year, $28.1 million deal.

"We're in a position now [as opposed to past seasons] where we can be thinking of development," Kerr said. "Not just for Yaxel, but our whole group. We are not in the [championship] conversation. So let's see what we can do as a group to kind of reestablish what we stand for and how we operate and new beginnings in a lot of ways. All of that is really exciting to me. And Yaxel's a big part of that."

Lendeborg has no issue embracing the spotlight and pressure. He has declared he can average 15 points, six rebounds and four assists in his first season. He believes he could win Rookie of the Year.

Asked during one of his many live streams this summer about Phoenix Suns wing Dillon Brooks, he responded: "I'm finna give Dillon Brooks belt, man. Stop playing." The Warriors face the Suns on Oct. 24, their third regular-season game.

"You can also see his youth with his comments in the media," Kerr said. "Our fans are going to love listening to him and he's going to say some stuff that he may have to retract and hold back. But I love it. I love him. I love guys like that. We always encourage everyone to be themselves and he's got a really great personality."

But that comes with an added spotlight, especially when playing for a brand like the Warriors next to a teammate like Curry.

"The nature of our league, social media and all the microscope is that they'll expect him to be a 20-8-6 guy right out the gate or whatever number you put on him," Curry said.

"But his job is to block all that out. He will know if he's impactful. He will know if he's helping win games. The stats and the numbers will follow. It's our job to protect him in that."

Still, the Warriors are struggling to contain their excitement and temper expectations for Lendeborg, who has popped off for 21 points, 18 rebounds, five assists and two blocks in his first 40 preseason minutes.

"He's obviously a winner," Curry said. "He had a successful year in college in the big role he had. He has great feel. He has great size. He's been shooting it really well. You can tell he wants to make the right play. For our offense and gameplan, that's usually going to shine."

stories.headline: Mikel Arteta: 'I still have the scar' from Arsenal's Champions League final defeat
stories.summary: Mikel Arteta has said he still has a "scar" from Arsenal's Champions League final defeat to Paris Saint-Germain in May.
stories.body:
Mikel Arteta has said he still has a "scar" from Arsenal's Champions League final defeat to Paris Saint-Germain in May.

The Spaniard, whose new four-year contract at the Emirates was announced on Wednesday, took the club to their first Champions League final for 20 years last season but saw his team defeated on penalties after a 1-1 draw.

Echoing the words of the last man to take them to the brink of elite European glory -- Arsène Wenger, who previously said that "every defeat is a scar in your heart" -- Arteta told The Athletic: "I still have the scar, like Arsène says.

"I still have that poison in my veins. It has to stay there because that's when you learn and that probably is going to be a massive driver for me and everybody."

Looking towards the future, Arteta added that he was excited for a number of different aspects of the club's growth.

"Globally, with our supporters? Great. How are we going to build the next three squads? Great. How the rules of the game are going to change us, and how we're going to stay ahead of that to take advantage? Great," he said.

"But this is going to happen if every single day we look after what we built. We make it a little bit better, like software that is upgrading and upgrading. When can it stop is infinite."

He added: "It feels like it's still a lot to do, and it's just the beginning."

Arteta has, however, already managed to do something no Arsenal manager had achieved for 22 years: win a league title.

"It wasn't just a trophy. It was a moment that we're going to remember for the rest of our lives," he said.

Asked what game from his Arsenal tenure he would relive, the 44-year-old chose the controversial 1-0 win over West Ham which put the Gunners on the brink of returning to the top of the perch.

"This is football elevated to its best version, when a journey, a moment that can change so many people's lives, goes one way or the other," he said. "You just pray because you know if it goes the wrong side, probably it's gone again.

"That day when I went home, I said, 'We're going to be champions. It is our year. This has happened for a reason, and we're going to get it done.'"
